extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP judges and policymakers
extracted.subtask_short: assessing prior art disclosure for patents
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining whether a piece of information constitutes prior art for novelty and inventive-step assessment, with country-specific rules (Spain, Sweden) and guidance on new media, evidence, temporal and territorial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art on novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The main effect of the prior art on the requisites of novelty and inventive activity is the determination that said invention cannot be patented if what is claimed were known previously (novelty) or if its content were evident for an expert in the matter (inventive activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art is a conjunct of information and knowledge used as a means of comparison. For novelty the object of the invention is compared to each element of the prior art; for inventive step the object is compared to the set of elements comprising the prior art to determine whether the invention would have been evident to a skilled person. A disclosure that does not completely anticipate may nonetheless be close enough to negate inventive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of pending/unpublished patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Published patent and utility-model applications filed before the filing date are considered prior art for novelty (Article 6.3 SPL / Art. 54.3 EPC), but unpublished patent or utility-model applications are not to be taken into account when assessing inventive activity (Article 8.2 SPL and Art. 56 EPC, final phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spanish practice excludes PCT applications that do not designate Spain from Article 6.3 SPL; European patent applications are included once the designation/fees are paid and the application is published. This distinction affects whether a specific prior filing can destroy novelty versus being relevant only for inventive-step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prior art / disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is 'everything that was accessible to the public prior to the patent application' (Article 6.2 SPL / Art. 54.2 EPC): 'through a written or verbal description, use or other means.' For utility models Spanish law limits prior art to disclosures 'in Spain'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concept of disclosure is interpreted as the mere possibility of accessing the background facts (accessibility), not actual knowledge. Disclosure must be proven using the evidence mechanisms in procedural law; courts/judges determine disclosure in case of doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of disclosure (including 'any other means')
rubrics_metrics.description: Means of disclosure are not limited to written or verbal information or use; the law expressly includes 'any other means' allowing public access (Article 6.2 SPL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European jurisprudence treats anything placed at the public's disposal as prior art regardless of how the public gained access. No special legal requisites are imposed for internet or data networks; the only common requisite is accessibility to the public. Practice lacks extensive jurisprudence on some novel means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of disclosure and grace-period exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule time elapsed since disclosure does not remove its relevance for novelty; however Spanish law (Article 7 SPL) provides three six-month exceptions where disclosures by the applicant do not destroy novelty: (a) evident abuse against the applicant, (b) exhibition at official or unofficially recognised expositions, (c) trials carried out by the applicant or causing parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions are limited to disclosures 'derived from the applicant's invention' and do not protect independent third-party disclosures. Spanish jurisprudence extends the exhibition exception beyond the 1928 Agreement to recognised local/national fairs. Time may still influence the assessment of inventive step (older disclosures may be less evident to skilled persons). Swedish practice treats time as generally irrelevant for novelty/non-obviousness, though time can be an indicator of non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure / territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents the place of disclosure is irrelevant because the novelty requirement is worldwide. For utility models the place matters: only disclosures made in Spain constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For internet disclosures the place of public access is considered to be where the computer terminal is installed. Whether a disclosure was intentional or accidental is generally irrelevant, except where Article 7(a) SPL (abuse) applies within the six-month exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal elements: applicant vs third-party disclosures and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation differentiates disclosing behaviour of the inventor/applicant versus third parties. Article 7 SPL grants time-benefit/exceptions to the applicant when disclosure occurred during the six months prior to filing in specific circumstances. There is no explicit SPL reference to disclosure by persons bound by confidentiality agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A breach of confidentiality may be considered a form of 'abuse' and thus fall under the six-month exception if it qualifies as 'evident abuse'. Spanish law does not provide a general protection for confidentiality beyond those exceptions; Swedish law likewise recognises the 'evident abuse' exception and exhibition exemption but states the grace-period concept is not broadly applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors and accidental disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidental disclosures (e.g., loss of documentation in public, erroneous publication) are generally treated as disclosures with prejudicial effect; there is no general juridical mechanism preventing the negative effects of such accidental disclosures except where the disclosure qualifies as abuse under Article 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erroneous publication of an application (e.g., after prior renunciation) can be especially damaging; applicants must take care to avoid unintended disclosures. Remedies may be civil (compensation) but do not automatically negate the prior-art effect unless abuse exception applies within prescribed time-limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient capacity and size of audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation does not require recipients to have a given capacity to understand the information; disclosure is determined by accessibility to the public — if a large or indefinite group had an opportunity to receive the information, disclosure has taken place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient that the opportunity to receive existed; actual comprehension is not necessary. Swedish practice emphasises whether the inventor controlled the information; number of recipients, their relation to the inventor, and confidentiality agreements are relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering / disassembly as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disassembly of embodiments and reverse engineering operations can provide information representing a disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical difficulty or time/effort required for reverse engineering is, in principle, not a reason to exclude that information from being 'publicly available' (Swedish application of EPO decisions such as G 1/92).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and new media disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Information made available on the Internet or electronic networks can be sufficient to affect novelty or inventive step, depending on content, who may access it, and the evidence available to prove disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no specific statutory requirements distinct from other forms of disclosure; however, differences arise in practice between public websites (accessible to the public) and communications like e-mail (sending to named recipients is not per se a disclosure). Proof of disclosure for internet material must be assessed case-by-case by courts; permanency, manipulation risk and timing create evidentiary challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality measures in electronic media (encryption, passwords, paywalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: If information is encrypted or access is password-restricted, on principle it is confidential and does not represent a disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access restrictions (passwords, paywalls) entail an obligation of confidentiality. Unauthorized access may lead to later disclosure, but that may be treated as an abuse against the applicant; the recipient and purpose of transmission are relevant. Swedish guidance similarly accepts electronic confidentiality measures if normal precautions are taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards and burden of proof for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party bears the burden of proving the facts it claims; Civil Procedural Law requires consideration of availability and facility of proof for each party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will require proof of existence, accessibility and disclosure. For internet disclosures, procedural rules or certificates from institutions managing the media (hosting providers, archives) would facilitate proof. There is no legal rule requiring different evidence standards for internet vs other media, but manipulation risks may demand careful evidentiary handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/duration and archival evidence for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory requirement regarding how long electronic information must remain accessible to qualify as disclosure; the moment of revelation (date of access) is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of existence and accessibility at the relevant date is necessary; maintaining archives or other records is desirable to meet evidentiary needs. Spanish law does not impose duration requirements, while procedural evidentiary tools are recommended to address loss or manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing/trials exemption conditions (Swedish and Spanish practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests or trials carried out by the applicant may not be deemed to destroy novelty under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spanish Article 7(c) and Swedish preparatory works set conditions: tests must not involve commercial offer or extensive public operation; Swedish guidance lists three conditions — (i) tests necessary to finish the invention, (ii) reasonable measures taken to restrict public access to information, and (iii) tests not carried out for longer or to a greater extent than defendable given the invention's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place/date specifics for internet disclosures (time-zone/whole-day rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A website accessible worldwide may produce different calendar dates of disclosure in different countries because of time zones; the place of disclosure for the internet is where the computer terminal is installed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether an internet disclosure occurred before a filing date, take into account time-zone differences and apply the 'whole day rule' as appropriate so that disclosure dates are correctly compared with filing/priority dates.
